opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, working with robots has made me deeply appreciate the human body in a way I never expected. When you spend decades trying to get a machine to do something as simple as pick up a cup, or fold a towel, or grasp an object it's never seen before, you start to realize how extraordinary the things we take for granted really are.

There's an idea called Moravec's paradox: the things that are hard for humans, like chess or calculus, turn out to be relatively easy for computers, while the things that are easy for us, like walking across a cluttered room or picking up a glass of water, are incredibly hard for robots. I've lived that paradox my whole career. A two-year-old can do things with their hands that the most advanced robot in the world still struggles with.

Part of what makes it so hard is the sheer richness of our bodies. Our skin has millions of sensors. Our hands have dozens of degrees of freedom, and our muscles and tendons are compliant, so they give a little and adapt when we make contact with something. Robots, by contrast, are mostly rigid, with fairly crude sensing. And there's so much uncertainty in the physical world: friction, the exact shape and weight of an object, tiny errors in perception. Humans handle all of that effortlessly, without even thinking about it.

So it's made me humble, and also a bit skeptical when people say robots are about to take over every job. I think we're making real progress, especially with new learning techniques, but there's a big gap between what people imagine and what robots can actually do. If anything, my work has given me a sense of awe for the human body. It's a remarkable machine, if you want to call it that, and we're still a long way from matching it.

r001.rationale: He says that decades of working with robots have made him appreciate how extraordinary the human body is, then describes its rich sensing, dexterity, and adaptability.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. You know, I've spent a long time now trying to get robots to do what seem like the simplest things – pick up a cup, fold a towel, grasp an object they've never seen before – and the honest answer is that it's made me much more humble about the human body, not less.

There's this phenomenon people sometimes call Moravec's paradox: the things that are hard for humans, like chess or calculus, turn out to be relatively easy for machines, and the things that are trivially easy for a two-year-old – reaching into a cluttered drawer and pulling out a pair of scissors – are extraordinarily hard for robots. And when you spend years on that problem, you start to look at your own hand differently. You notice that you don't think about it. You just reach, and your fingers conform to the object, and the skin deforms, and there's all this tactile feedback arriving continuously, and your arm compensates for errors before you're even consciously aware of them. We can't do that yet. Not even close.

So one thing it's done is made me really attentive to uncertainty. In robotics, uncertainty is the central problem – uncertainty in sensing, uncertainty in control, uncertainty in the physics of contact. And the human body is this incredible system for living gracefully with uncertainty. It's not precise, actually. If you measure human motion it's quite sloppy. But it's robust. It recovers. It improvises. I think the body is less like a precision machine and more like a jazz musician, and that's been a real shift for me.

The other thing – and this is maybe a bit more philosophical – is that it's made me skeptical of the idea that the body is just a vehicle for the brain. There's a tendency, especially in AI, to think intelligence is all in the head and the body is incidental. But when you work on robots you see how much of what we'd call intelligence is distributed into the structure of the body itself. The compliance of your fingertips does computation, in a sense. The way your tendons are arranged solves problems so your brain doesn't have to. So I've come to think of the body as part of the mind, not separate from it. And robots, in their clumsiness, are a kind of mirror that lets us see what we've been taking for granted all along.

r001.rationale: Goldberg says that spending years trying to make robots perform simple tasks has made him more humble about the human body, then describes its intricate sensing, movement, and recovery abilities.

astra-6.text:
Working with robots has given me a much deeper appreciation for the human body, especially our hands. We can pick up a set of keys, find the right one, and put it into a lock while carrying on a conversation. But when you try to get a robot to do that, you discover how much perception and control is involved: sensing contact, adjusting your grip, responding when something slips.

That’s a recurring experience in robotics. Something that seems simple turns out to be extraordinarily subtle. So rather than making me see the body as just a machine, the work has made me more aware of how remarkable our everyday abilities are.

r001.rationale: He says robotics repeatedly reveals how much subtle perception and control underlie simple abilities, giving him deeper appreciation for the body.

sol-6.1.text:
Working with robots has given me a much greater appreciation for the human body. You try to get a robot to do something that seems very simple—pick up a glass, say—and you discover how much is involved. You have to sense where the glass is, work out how to approach it, and adjust your grip as you make contact. We do all of that without really thinking about it.

The hand is particularly remarkable. It’s flexible, it’s sensitive, and it can handle an extraordinary variety of objects. When you try to reproduce even a small part of that capability, you start seeing everyday human actions differently. Things we take for granted become quite astonishing.

r001.rationale: Goldberg says working with robots has increased his appreciation for the body, explaining that attempts to reproduce simple actions reveal how much sensing and adjustment they require. He describes this as changing how he sees everyday actions, conveying a recurring reminder of the body’s complexity.
